name: observer
intent: Let a subject inform an open-ended set of dependents about its state changes through a one-way subscription, so the subject never has to know which objects react or how many there are.
problem: One state change has to reach many dependents whose identities are not known when the subject is written: polling the subject wastes work in every dependent, and hard-wiring the dependents into the subject couples it to every consumer, so a new reaction means editing the subject and adding a call the subject should not know about.
context: Applies when one object owns state (or emits events) that several others must track - model and views, repository and caches, aggregate and audit/projection handlers - and the set of subscribers is dynamic: registered and removed at runtime by their own lifecycle. It also applies to in-process event fan-out where the alternative is polling or a compile-time call list, and the reaction may be slower than the change.
benefits: Dependents subscribe and unsubscribe at runtime; the subject and its existing callers need no modification when a new reaction appears (open/closed for observers).

The subject depends only on an abstract update operation (interface, function type, delegate, callable), so it does not know the concrete observer types and observers can be contributed by other modules or teams.
Notification is one-way broadcast: observers cannot reply, so no request/response protocol, no return-value coupling and no result aggregation creep into the change path.
Subscription is dynamic, which matches transient participants - a dialog, a request-scoped cache, a job's progress reporter - that exist only for part of the subject's lifetime.
The registry and the dispatch policy live in one place, so ordering, replay, filtering and delivery strategy can be centralised instead of being re-implemented per dependent.
tradeoffs: Updates cascade: a notification can make an observer change another subject, which notifies again; the subject cannot see where the chain ends and the control flow that matters is no longer visible in the call graph.

Every observer registered for a change is notified of it, including changes it does not care about, and the classic update signature often says nothing about what changed, so observers re-read the subject to find out.

Notification order is unspecified in the pattern (registration order in the usual list-based realizations), and a notification raised from inside a notification loops or corrupts state unless re-entrancy is explicitly handled.
Classic registries hold strong references: a forgotten unsubscribe keeps the observer - and everything it holds - alive, the classic listener leak in UI toolkits and long-lived services.

Observers run in the subject's call stack, so one slow or throwing observer delays or breaks the others, and a synchronous fan-out turns a cheap state change into an O(observers) operation with no backpressure.

Thread safety becomes a shared obligation: subject and observers must agree who synchronises what, and notifying while holding the subject's lock deadlocks as soon as a handler subscribes or notifies.

participants.responsibility: Owns the subscription registry, exposes attach/detach, and notifies every registered dependent after a change; it knows only the abstract observer operation, never concrete observer types.
Holds the state of interest, decides when a change is worth announcing, and triggers the notification (often the same object as the Subject, or the Subject composed into it).
Declares the update/notification operation - one method in the classic form - that the subject calls; all observers are interchangeable through this interface.
Reacts to the notification, usually by pulling the changed state it needs from the subject or from the event payload, and keeps its own state consistent with it.
Carries the change into the callback - the subject reference, an event name plus payload, or a typed event object - so observers get context without a permanent back-reference to the subject.

use_cases: Model/view synchronisation: a model notifies the widgets, forms and charts that display it without the model depending on any view (MVC/MVVM/Flux-style state containers).
In-process domain events: an aggregate publishes something-happened events that audit logging, read-model projections and notification handlers subscribe to without the aggregate knowing them.
Cache and derived-data invalidation: a cache subscribes to the repository or configuration object it derives from and drops or recomputes entries when that state changes.
Configuration and feature-flag propagation: a config object notifies components that must re-read values or reconfigure when settings change at runtime.
Progress and telemetry fan-out: a long-running task publishes progress or readings to a logger, a progress indicator and a metrics collector at the same time.
Framework hooks: a container or server publishes lifecycle events (started, request finished, session closed) that application components attach to through the framework's event facility.

Reactive Extensions (RxPY, RxJS, Rx.NET): the Observer pattern generalised into composable event streams — Observable sequences pushed over time, transformed by operators (map, filter, debounce, throttle, buffer, merge) and consumed by Observers, with explicit Subscription/disposable lifecycle and Scheduler-based concurrency control.

Event-driven microservices with durable event buses: domain events published by a service are consumed by Kafka topics or Redis Streams; the observer relationship (single-process, synchronous, subject-knows-observers) scales to a broker-mediated pattern (Pub/Sub, asynchronous, producers-and-consumers-unaware) while preserving the same mental model.

Real-time push and streaming APIs: Server-Sent Events (SSE) and WebSocket connections use an implicit Observer pattern where the client subscribes to a server-side event source; connection lifecycle, heartbeat management and backpressure via client-driven polling map directly to the subscribe/dispose/request cycle.

Reactive GUI state management: React hooks (useEffect + event sources), Vue refs/reactive objects, Jetpack Compose state hoisting, and Flutter StreamBuilder are all language-specific realisations of the Observer contract — a widget or component observes a mutable state holder and re-renders when the holder notifies of a change.

Micro-frontend communication: independent micro-frontend applications share an event bus rather than importing each other's code directly, keeping teams decoupled while allowing selective event-driven coordination.

Real-time collaborative editing: an operational-transform or CRDT-based editor propagates remote mutations as observer events to local UI components; conflict resolution and cursor broadcast are observer-style fan-outs from a single document subject.

Java Flow API: java.util.concurrent.Flow.Publisher, Flow.Subscriber and Flow.Subscription provide an Observer-style one-to-many push contract with ordered per-subscriber delivery, explicit cancellation, completion/error signals and demand control; use it when a typed stream needs backpressure rather than a raw callback list.

Browser DOM events: EventTarget.addEventListener/removeEventListener let components observe typed event sources, while AbortSignal removes listeners as a lifecycle ends; use this built-in subject/listener contract instead of inventing a registry for UI and platform events.
avoid_when: One known consumer with a fixed relationship: a direct method call (or a plain callback parameter) is simpler and keeps the control flow visible in the code.
The set of reactions is fixed, small and local: a straight-line call sequence is easier to read, test and debug than a registry nobody can enumerate.
Observers must answer, aggregate results or transform the notification: use Command/Mediator, a future/CompletableFuture or a request/response channel instead of a one-way broadcast.

Notification must survive process restarts or broker failure, or cross a process boundary: in-process observers do not - use a message channel with delivery guarantees (Publish-Subscribe Channel, Guaranteed Delivery).

Very high update rates with many observers that only care about a fraction of the changes: the O(observers) fan-out and re-reading cost more than a pull-based design or a stream with backpressure and filtering.
anti_patterns: Notification storms: an observer notifies another subject from inside its update, so two publishers feed each other and the cascade only shows up under load.
The god event manager: every component subscribes to one global bus for everything, turning the subscription list into an invisible call graph that no one can enumerate.
Strong-reference registries without unsubscribe discipline: the subject keeps dead observers alive and keeps calling them - the classic listener leak of long-lived UI services.
Blocking work inside the notification: handlers perform I/O or long computation in the subject's call stack, so one slow observer stalls the subject and every observer behind it.
Using Observer where a Mediator is wanted: with every component publishing and subscribing to every other, the many-to-many dependency that motivated the design is back, only hidden.

Notification order assumed deterministic: code that depends on observers firing in registration order, or that encodes ordering as a side-effect of subscription sequence, breaks when the registry implementation changes, collection semantics differ, or threads schedule differently — make observers order-independent or document an explicit ordering contract.

WeakReference as a substitute for explicit unsubscribe discipline: weak references trade a deterministic memory leak (observers stay alive until explicitly removed) for a non-deterministic one (observers are collected whenever GC runs, with no guarantee of prompt cleanup); if an observer is only held by the subject and nothing else, a forgotten strong reference elsewhere defeats the mitigation entirely.

Re-entrancy loops from observers mutating the subject mid-notification: an observer's update handler calls back into the subject (directly or via another subject), triggering a nested notification before the outer one completes; observers then see intermediate state, and deeply nested updates can exhaust the stack — defer mutations from inside handlers using a queue, async executor, or explicit re-entrancy guard.

Over-notifying on every intermediate state change: emitting for every keystroke or micro-step overwhelms observers and amplifies fan-out cost; batch or debounce notifications when only the final state matters.

Leaking subscription references in framework components: discarding the returned unsubscribe/dispose handle (from addEventListener, subscribe, or useEffect without a cleanup return) makes the observer immortal — the dominant memory leak pattern in React, Vue, Angular and vanilla DOM codebases.

Using Observer for commands: emitting 'saveOrder' as an event is a command, not a fact; observers should react to events (OrderCreated), not execute actions; commands belong in a command bus or direct method call with a clear return value.

Anonymous function observers that cannot be individually removed: lambdas and inline closures cannot be unsubscribed without storing a reference, forcing blanket clear-all strategies that break other subscribers.
design_principles: Program to an interface, not an implementation: the subject depends on the abstract update operation, not on concrete subscribers.
Open/closed principle: new reactions arrive by subscription, so neither the subject nor existing observers change.
Single responsibility: the subject owns state and broadcast, each observer owns its own reaction.
Inversion of control (Hollywood principle): the framework or subject calls the observer, not the observer the subject.
Separation of concerns: producing a change and reacting to it are decoupled in code and in time.

Explicit over implicit: name event types explicitly (typed interfaces or string constants) rather than relying on observer identity or subscription order to route notifications — makes the system introspectable and grep-able.
best_practices: Notify only after the state transition is complete and consistent, so a handler that reads the subject back sees the new value.
Iterate over a snapshot of the registry and make subscribe/unsubscribe from inside a handler well-defined (defer the mutation or document the snapshot semantics).
Return a removal handle (id, Disposable, Cancellable, token, unsubscribe closure) from subscribe and release it in the same lifecycle that acquired it.
Prefer weak references, or an explicit teardown owned by the subject, for observers whose lifetime the subject does not own.
State the threading contract explicitly: which thread notifies, who may subscribe concurrently, and that notification never happens while holding the subject's lock.
Keep handlers short, non-blocking and non-throwing; isolate or log exceptions per observer so one failure does not abort the remaining notifications.
Pass the payload with the notification (event object or old/new values) instead of forcing every observer to re-read the subject.
Bound the fan-out on hot paths: filter by event type or interest, and use a queue or channel with an explicit drop policy when observers can be slow.

Prefer weak references (WeakReference, WeakHashMap, or language equivalents) for observers whose lifetime the subject does not own, so a forgotten unsubscribe does not prevent garbage collection — but document this tradeoff explicitly because GC timing becomes non-deterministic and a strong reference held elsewhere still defeats the mitigation.

Use a thread-safe collection (CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet, or equivalent) for the observer registry when subscription and notification can occur from multiple threads; iterate a snapshot of the registry and make Subscribe/Dispose mutually exclusive with notification.

Pass a typed event object (or old/new value pair) with the notification instead of forcing every observer to re-read the subject — this keeps the subject's internal state encapsulated and makes the notification self-contained, testable and introspectable.

Attach an IObserver<T> instance to only one IObservable<T> provider; if a subscriber must track multiple sources, use separate observer instances or a composite observer that dispatches to domain-specific handlers rather than one object multiplexing all event types.

Handle exceptions as informational: log or record them per-observer and continue notifying remaining observers rather than letting one throwing handler abort the entire fan-out; after OnError or OnCompleted the provider unsubscribes all observers and emits no further notifications.

In async systems, prefer concurrent fan-out (asyncio.gather with return_exceptions=True or equivalent) so one slow I/O-bound observer does not block faster observers behind it — but keep synchronous in-memory observers on the synchronous path; do not pay the async overhead when observers are just CPU work.

Use AbortSignal (EventTarget) or framework-provided lifecycle hooks (React useEffect cleanup, Vue onUnmounted, Angular DestroyRef) to tie subscriptions to component lifetimes — a single abort() or framework cleanup call removes all listeners at once rather than tracking each handle individually.

Avoid emitting stringly-typed events; define event interfaces or enum-like constants so event names are validated and refactorable; typos become compile-time or linter errors instead of silent failures.

Distinguish hot from cold observables: a hot observable (like a DOM EventTarget or a live stream) emits regardless of subscription count; a cold observable (like an HTTP response or file read) replays its sequence to each subscriber from the start. Choose or document which you are exposing so consumers understand whether they receive historical events on subscription.

For typed reactive streams with backpressure (ReactiveX, Java Flow, Project Reactor), expose IObservable or equivalent rather than a raw callback registry so consumers can use map, filter, debounce, switchMap and cancellation operators declaratively.

Prefer one-shot finite observables (Promise-equivalent) when the notification genuinely happens once; Reserve the continuous observer for genuinely repeated events — mixing them forces consumers to handle completion unnecessarily or leaks subscriptions.

In performance-sensitive paths, consider scheduling notifications via queueMicrotask or setTimeout(0) to avoid blocking the call stack on each notification; batch or debounce high-frequency events (mouse move, scroll, telemetry) rather than notifying on every micro-step.
sources: Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) - Observer (Behavioral Patterns; also known as Dependents, Publish-Subscribe).
https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/observer
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/events-overview

Microsoft .NET Team, "Observer Design Pattern Best Practices" (learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/events/observer-design-pattern-best-practices) — covers thread-safe Subscribe/Dispose, typed notification payloads, IObservable<T>/IObserver<T> contracts, and when to prefer events, IAsyncEnumerable, Channels, or Rx.NET over a raw implementation.

Microsoft .NET Docs, "Weak Event Patterns" (learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/events/weak-event-patterns) — four implementation strategies for the weak event pattern (existing WeakEventManager, generic WeakEventManager<T>, custom WeakEventManager, third-party), with full WPF template code and guidance on when each approach applies.

ReactiveX, "Observable" (reactivex.io/documentation/observable.html) — the canonical reference for Reactive Extensions; defines the Observable contract (onNext, onError, onCompleted), backpressure philosophy, hot vs cold observables, and the operator composition model that extends the classic Observer pattern into composable event streams.

RxJS Team, "RxJS Guide" (rxjs.dev/guide/overview) — RxJS as a production-grade Observer implementation: Observable/Observer/Subscription/Subject/Operator/Scheduler model, pipe-based composition, schedulers for concurrency control, and guidance on when RxJS suits a problem vs plain callbacks.

RxPY Authors, "RxPY Documentation" (rxpy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) — RxPY for Python, covering Subject variants (Subject, BehaviorSubject, ReplaySubject, AsyncSubject), operators, schedulers, asyncio integration, and best practices for keeping Rx at system boundaries rather than domain logic.

Garrett Mills, "Deprecating the Observer Pattern" (software patterns lexicon / arxiv) — academic critique of the Observer pattern (Gamma et al.) covering: side-effects from stateless observers, encapsulation violations, composition difficulty, resource management burden, and semantic distance from programmer intent; proposes reactive signals as an alternative.

Thinking in Python, "Observer — Thinking in Python" (thinkinginpython.com/30_Patterns--Observer.html) — Pythonic callable-based observer with property setters, async fan-out via asyncio.gather, re-entrancy guards, WeakValueDictionary/WeakMethod for memory-safe subscriptions, and catch-collect-continue exception handling.

Patterns.dev, "Observer Pattern" (patterns.dev/vanilla/observer-pattern/) — modern JS/TS implementation using Set for O(1) unsubscribe, AbortSignal integration with EventTarget for one-line cleanup, Pub/Sub vs Observer distinction, signals as a TC39 proposal convergence, and RxJS for complex async stream composition (debounce, switchMap, distinctUntilChanged).

Artem Khrienov, "The Observer Pattern in Modern JavaScript: Building Reactive Systems" (medium.com/@artemkhrenov, 2025) — class-based and functional Observer in JavaScript, EventEmitter with once() and typed event routing, Observable class with map/filter operators, subscription teardown and safeObserver wrappers for unsubscribe/error/complete lifecycle.

Mathias Paulenko, "Implement Reactive Systems with the Observer Pattern" (stackpractices.com/recipes/observer-pattern-recipe/, 2026) — production-grade event emitter with typed events, async Promise.all emit, hot vs cold observables, RxPY reactive streams, deadlock/cycle detection, priority execution, dead-letter queues, and hybrid in-process + Kafka fan-out for microservices.

Paul Serban, "Comparing Observer and Publish-Subscribe Design Patterns" (paulserban.eu/blog/post/comparing-observer-and-publish-subscribe-design-patterns/, 2022) — architectural comparison: Observer (Subject owns registry, direct synchronous call, single-process) vs Pub/Sub (broker mediates, asynchronous, cross-process); memory leak and lapsed listener risks; message delivery guarantees; maintenance overhead of spooky-action-at-a-distance in global event buses.

Phillip Johnston, "Differentiating Observer and Publish-Subscribe Patterns" (embeddedartistry.com/fieldatlas/differentiating-observer-and-publish-subscribe-patterns/, 2022) — argues Observer and Pub/Sub are the same pattern at different implementation levels; examines synchronous vs asynchronous delivery, the ChangeManager in GoF as a primitive broker, and the coupling equivalence of subject-broker and broker-observer relationships.

Stack Overflow, "Pub/Sub Vs Observer Vs Reactive" (stackoverflow.com/questions/30784360) — ReactiveX asObserver + pull (Iterator duality); reactive programming is declarative data-flow on push-based streams; Pub/Sub scalability through async broker decoupling vs Observer's single-process performance.

Codemia, "Event driven microservices with message brokers vs reactive programming" (codemia.io/knowledge-hub/path/event_driven_microservices) — Kafka (Pub/Sub, durable, high-throughput) vs RxJava/Project Reactor (Observer pattern extended with backpressure, composable operators) vs RSocket (binary protocol with built-in backpressure for request-stream and channel models); synergy of Kafka for fan-out + Reactor for in-service stream transformation.

JSdev.space, "Observer vs Publish-Subscribe: What's the Difference?" (jsdev.space/observer-vs-publish-subscribe-pattern/, 2026) — direct Observer coupling vs broker-mediated Pub/Sub; micro-frontend use-case for Pub/Sub; framework-specific patterns (Redux/Zustand/MobX stores as Observer, React useSyncExternalStore, Angular takeUntilDestroyed); signals (Solid, Vue Reactivity, TC39 proposal) as fine-grained Observer alternative.

Software Engineering Stack Exchange, "Should event listeners be held in weak references?" (softwareengineering.stackexchange.com/questions/238753) — strong references for promise chains (short-lived); weak references trade deterministic leaks for non-deterministic GC timing; explicit unsubscribe + RAII/destructors as the correct solution, weak references as a band-aid.

Ko-Hsin Liang, "Frontend Memory Leaks: A 500-Repository Static Analysis and Five-Scenario Benchmark Study" (stackinsight.dev/blog/memory-leak-empirical-study/, 2026) — empirical study finding: missing timer cleanup (43.9%), missing event listener removal (19.0%), missing subscription cleanup (13.9%), missing useEffect cleanup (9.3%), missing Vue watch stop handle (7.1%); each leak pattern retains ~8 KB per navigation cycle; audit and fix priority order.

Memory Leak Guide, "Event Listener Memory Leaks" (memory-leak.khuong.dev/patterns/event-listeners.html) — Angular takeUntilDestroyed pattern, React useEffect cleanup returns, Vue beforeUnmount cleanup, async pipe for Angular (markForCheck + OnPush compatibility), long-lived service subscription leaks, Zone.js monkey-patch retention risks.

Stack Overflow, "Clean JavaFX property listeners and bindings" (stackoverflow.com/questions/14558266) — JavaFX WeakListener/WeakInvalidationListener for automatic cleanup; WeakReference band-aid limitations; unbind() necessity for BooleanPropertyBase (leak fixed in Java 9); per-binding empty WeakReference accumulation as a subtle memory leak.

Ilyas Talib, "Observer Pattern and Lapsed Listener Problem" (ilkinulas.github.io/development/general/2016/04/17/observer-pattern.html) — lapsed listener problem in Java/C# with strong references; WeakReference implementation of observer registry; dangling pointer risk in C++ if observer deleted without unregistering.

Observer | Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (GoF catalog excerpt) — defines the one-to-many dependency and automatic notification that anchor the pattern's canonical origin. (https://flylib.com/books/en/2.505.1.29/1/)

Oracle Java SE 21, Flow.Publisher — official Java reactive-streams contract: a publisher sends ordered items to multiple Flow.Subscriber instances, with Flow.Subscription controlling demand and cancellation. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/Flow.Publisher.html

MDN, EventTarget.addEventListener() — official browser API documentation for registering listeners and tying removal to AbortSignal; a concrete Observer-style event source with lifecycle cleanup. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/EventTarget/addEventListener

EPFL Infoscience, "Deprecating the Observer Pattern" — critiques hidden side effects, encapsulation and composition problems, and the explicit disposal/resource-management burden. https://infoscience.epfl.ch/handle/20.500.14299/49107
